    title: 'Sharing State Between Micro-Frontends: Solving the Deployment Coupling Trap',
    excerpt: 'A senior-level engineering case study on moving from monolithic shared state to event-driven communication to preserve team independence in enterprise micro-frontend architectures.',

    content: `
      <h1>Sharing State Between Micro-<a href="/blog/b2b-saas-frontend-architecture-multi-tenant-scale">b2b saas frontend</a>: Solving the Deployment Coupling Trap</h1><p>In large-scale enterprise environments, the promise of micro-frontends is team independence. However, most teams fall into the 'Deployment Coupling' trap by attempting to share a single global state store across independent bundles. This case study analyzes how we transitioned a financial dashboard serving 2.8M monthly requests from a brittle shared Redux architecture to a resilient, event-driven stream using RxJS and the CustomEvent API.</p><h3>How do you share state between micro-frontends without tight coupling?</h3><p><strong>To effectively achieve sharing state between micro-frontends, engineers should implement an event-driven architecture using the browser's native CustomEvent API or RxJS streams. This approach utilizes a 'Pub-Sub' model where micro-frontends emit and listen for specific events, ensuring domain isolation and preventing the 'deployment coupling' trap common with shared global stores.</strong></p><ul><li>Use the <code>window</code> object as a message bus for <code>CustomEvents</code>.</li><li>Implement RxJS <code>BehaviorSubject</code> for reactive state persistence.</li><li>Define strict TypeScript interfaces for event payloads.</li><li>Ensure 100% cleanup of listeners during unmounting to prevent memory leaks.</li><li>Leverage <a href="https://webpack.js.org/concepts/module-federation/">module federation</a> for shared dependencies but keep runtimes isolated.</li></ul><h2>1. INCIDENT REPORT: THE VERSIONING COLLISION</h2><p>At FouriqTech, we were managing a multi-tenant B2B platform where the shell (host) and four remote micro-frontends shared a unified Redux store. During a staggered rollout in the EMEA region, Team A deployed a breaking schema change to the <code>user_session</code> slice in the User-Profile MFE. Because the Global-Header MFE relied on the same Redux store instance, it failed to hydrate the profile data, causing a total UI crash (White Screen of Death) for 14.2% of active users. The p95 recovery time was 42 minutes because a rollback of the Remote also required a rollback of the Host due to the shared state dependency.</p><h2>2. WRONG ASSUMPTIONS</h2><p>Initially, the engineering team assumed that <a href="/blog/fixing-slow-nextjs-monorepo-build-enterprise-case-study">fixing slow monorepo builds</a> and using Module Federation's <code>shared</code> configuration would be enough. We believed that by sharing <code><a href="/blog/react-form-performance-optimization-enterprise-guide">react form performance</a>-redux</code> as a singleton, we were optimizing performance. We ignored the fact that while the *library* was a singleton, the *state schema* was a hidden contract that required perfectly synchronized deployments—defeating the primary purpose of <a href="/blog/b2b-<a href="/services/custom-saas-platform-development">saas</a>-frontend-architecture-multi-tenant-scale">multi-tenant frontend architecture</a>.</p><h2>3. DEBUGGING PROCESS</h2><p>We utilized OpenTelemetry to trace state hydration across the runtime integration. We observed that the Host application was attempting to access <code>state.auth.user.v2_metadata</code> while the Remote was still providing <code>state.auth.user.v1_data</code>. </p><p>Tools used for isolation:</p><ul><li><strong>Chrome DevTools Protocol:</strong> Monitored the memory heap and identified that the shared store was retaining references to unmounted micro-frontends.</li><li><strong>Redux DevTools:</strong> Revealed that actions dispatched from one MFE were triggering expensive re-renders in unrelated MFEs, leading to <a href="/blog/fix-react-main-thread-blocking-dashboard-inp">main thread blocking issues</a> and high Interaction to Next Paint (INP) scores exceeding 450ms.</li></ul><h2>4. ROOT CAUSE</h2><p>The technical failure was **Runtime Integration Tight Coupling**. By sharing a single Redux store, we created a single point of failure. Micro-frontends were no longer independent; they were 'distributed monoliths.' Any change to the shared state tree required a coordinated release, which is the antithesis of micro-frontend orchestration. The lack of an isolation layer meant that a version mismatch in the state schema resulted in a runtime exception rather than a graceful degradation.</p><h2>5. IMPLEMENTATION FIX: THE REACTIVE EVENT BUS</h2><p>We replaced the shared store with an <strong>Event Bus Pattern</strong> using <a href="https://rxjs.dev/guide/overview">RxJS</a> and native <code>CustomEvent</code>. This established a <strong>frontend decoupling</strong> layer where MFEs communicate via asynchronous message passing rather than direct state access.</p><pre><code>// The Core Event Bus Service
import { Subject, filter, map } from 'rxjs';

interface MfeEvent {
  type: string;
  payload: any;
  source: string;
}

class GlobalBus {
  private static instance: GlobalBus;
  private bus$ = new Subject&lt;MfeEvent&gt;();

  public static getInstance() {
    if (!window.__FouriqBus) {
      window.__FouriqBus = new GlobalBus();
    }
    return window.__FouriqBus;
  }

  emit(event: MfeEvent) {
    this.bus$.next(event);
    // Fallback for non-RxJS micro-frontends
    window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('mfe-communication', { detail: event }));
  }

  on(eventType: string) {
    return this.bus$.asObservable().pipe(
      filter(e =&gt; e.type === eventType),
      map(e =&gt; e.payload)
    );
  }
}</code></pre><p>In the React micro-frontend, we implemented a custom hook with mandatory cleanup to prevent the memory leaks identified in our debugging:</p><pre><code>export const useMfeState = (eventType, initialState) => {
  const [state, setState] = useState(initialState);

  useEffect(() => {
    const bus = GlobalBus.getInstance();
    const subscription = bus.on(eventType).subscribe(setState);
    
    return () => subscription.unsubscribe(); // CRITICAL: Prevent memory leaks
  }, [eventType]);

  return state;
};</code></pre><h2>6. MEASURED RESULTS</h2><p>The transition to an event-driven model for <strong>sharing state between micro-frontends</strong> yielded significant performance and stability gains:</p><ul><li><strong>Deployment Failure Rate:</strong> Dropped from 14.2% to &lt;0.05% (no more version collisions).</li><li><strong>Build Speed:</strong> Independent bundles reduced the host build time by 65%.</li><li><strong>Runtime Performance:</strong> State propagation latency reduced from 220ms (via Redux middleware) to ~12ms using RxJS streams.</li><li><strong>Memory Footprint:</strong> Heap usage per MFE decreased by 30MB by eliminating redundant shared dependencies.</li></ul><h2>7. UNEXPECTED PROBLEM: EVENT RACE CONDITIONS</h2><p>After the fix, we encountered an issue where the Header MFE would emit a <code>USER_LOADED</code> event before the Sidebar MFE had finished mounting, causing the Sidebar to miss the initial state. We mitigated this by introducing a <strong>reactive state</strong> layer using <code>BehaviorSubject</code> in our bus, which ensures that new subscribers immediately receive the 'last known good' value upon subscription.</p><h2>8. REQUEST LIFECYCLE BREAKDOWN</h2><ol><li><strong>Micro-Frontend Mount:</strong> The Remote MFE registers with the <code>GlobalBus</code>.</li><li><strong>Subscription (15ms):</strong> The MFE subscribes to specific event streams (e.g., <code>ORG_CHANGED</code>).</li><li><strong>State Propagation (2ms):</strong> The Host emits a change via the <code>postMessage API</code> or internal RxJS bus.</li><li><strong>Local Reconciliation (8ms):</strong> The MFE receives the payload and updates its local <a href="/blog/managing-complex-state-react-enterprise-case-study">complex state</a>.</li><li><strong>UI Update:</strong> React performs a targeted re-render confined to the specific MFE domain.</li></ol><h2>9. TRADE-OFF ANALYSIS</h2><p>While this approach solves deployment coupling, it introduces <strong>Eventual Consistency</strong>. Unlike Redux, where state changes are atomic and immediate, event-driven state can have a slight lag (10-20ms) across different MFEs. For high-frequency trading dashboards or real-time collaborative editors, this may require additional sequence numbers or timestamps to handle out-of-order messages. For 95% of enterprise <a href="/services/custom-saas-platform-development">saas</a> applications, the trade-off for team independence is worth the complexity.</p><h2>10. STRONG OPINION</h2><p>If you are using a shared Redux or MobX store for **sharing state between micro-frontends**, you do not have micro-frontends; you have a distributed monolith that is exponentially harder to maintain than a standard one. Architectural purity at FouriqTech demands that micro-frontends share *events*, not *objects*. If your MFE cannot function when the rest of the application is offline or on a different version, your isolation strategy has failed.</p>
